https://baltic-review.com/tartu-meeting-.text: Share Tweet 0 Rural energy initiatives are being examined as part of an international meeting in Tartu. From energy idea to local practice Estonia is hosting a timely international discussion about one of the most practical questions in the clean-energy transition: how can rural communities move from individual renewable-energy projects to locally organised systems that deliver lasting benefits? The question is at the centre of the EC4RURAL project’s annual meeting in Tartu on 23–24 September 2026. The gathering brings together project partners working with rural municipalities and communities in Estonia and Galicia, Spain. According to the project announcement by the Galician Federation of Municipalities and Provinces, the meeting is being used to compare pilot experiences, identify obstacles and discuss how local energy communities can remain active beyond the initial project period. The event is taking place as Estonia’s own debate about community energy becomes more concrete. The University of Tartu and the Estonian University of Life Sciences recently hosted a separate conference on 22 September focused on how solar-energy communities can move from an idea to an operating model. That conference presented practical tools for assessing feasibility, financing and cooperation between local authorities, residents, apartment associations, businesses and researchers. Why rural communities matter Energy communities are designed to give local people a more active role in renewable-energy production and use. They can bring together households, companies, municipalities or civic organisations around solar installations, storage, energy efficiency or local energy planning. In rural areas, the model can connect energy policy with wider questions of development. A village may be interested not only in producing electricity, but also in lowering the cost of operating a community building, supporting local businesses, improving the energy performance of homes or retaining more value within the local economy. The EC4RURAL meeting reflects that broader approach. The project’s Estonian partners include the University of Tartu, the Estonian Association of Cities and Municipalities, the Tartu Regional Energy Agency and the Estonian Leader Union. The University of Tartu’s project information says the work is intended to strengthen relationships between municipalities and rural communities while ensuring that less-developed and peripheral areas can participate in the energy transition. Learning from local pilots The Tartu programme includes an exchange of experience between Estonian and Galician pilot areas. It also includes a technical visit to Põltsamaa, where participants are examining local renewable-energy initiatives, the Umbusi community and the work of the Jõgevamaa Cooperation Centre, which supports measures designed to reduce energy costs. That emphasis on visiting operating or emerging initiatives is important. Community energy is often discussed through national targets and large infrastructure, but its success also depends on smaller decisions: who owns an installation, who can use the electricity, how costs are shared, and whether local residents have enough information to take part. Recent reporting by Estonia’s public broadcaster ERR has highlighted the same practical dimension. Participants in a 22 September conference in Tartu described local energy communities as responses to specific needs, such as high electricity costs or the desire to make better use of locally generated solar power. The report also noted that communities continue to face regulatory and technical barriers, including restrictions on sharing surplus electricity through the grid. A constructive test for the transition The Tartu meeting is therefore less about presenting a single universal model than about testing what can work in different places. Rural communities vary in population, infrastructure, income and access to technical expertise. A solution suitable for a village in southern Estonia may need to be adapted elsewhere. That flexibility is also the project’s constructive contribution. By combining municipal knowledge, research, community experience and European cooperation, EC4RURAL is treating the energy transition as a social and organisational process as well as a technological one. The meeting’s second day is dedicated to future planning, project indicators, resources and the continuation of results. For Estonia, the significance lies in whether the lessons gathered in Tartu can help more communities evaluate realistic projects, avoid unnecessary complexity and develop renewable energy around local priorities. Community energy will not replace national grids or larger renewable projects. It can, however, give rural residents a clearer role in the transition and help connect climate goals with everyday concerns such as household bills, local services and regional resilience. https://www.dw.com/en/trump-s-diesel-dea.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OF6H Diesel supplies are under pressure and analysts are skeptical Trump's diesel deal with Russia will lower prices Image: Patrick T. Fallon/AFP Advertisement With or without a deal with Russia, diesel prices on global markets are unlikely to fall significantly anytime soon. That is the assessment of experts interviewed by DW regarding the latest fuel-supply agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin . "The main reason for high diesel prices is the war in Iran and the simultaneous disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait," said Samina Sultan, a foreign trade expert at the German Economic Institute (IW) in Cologne. The situation has led to production outages and made fuel shipments "more expensive, less secure and more difficult," she said. Trump's deal with Russia also has an additional geopolitical dimension, Sultan said: "It causes the wars in Ukraine and Iran to become completely intertwined." Wars reducing refinery output Things are looking up, though. Roughly 13.5 million barrels of crude oil are once again flowing through the Strait of Hormuz a day, according to shipping and commodities analytics firm Kpler. But for refined products such as diesel, volumes remain far lower at around 677,000 barrels per day, compared with 3.6 million barrels before the war. Carsten Fritsch, a commodities analyst at Commerzbank, also attributes the price increases to the wars. "If nothing changes in Ukraine and the Middle East, I see very few ways to resolve these supply bottlenecks," he said. Trump expects prices to fall at record speed In a social media post on October 9, Trump announced that he would temporarily suspend some sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel. He wrote "diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" in a mix of lowercase and all caps. Russia confirmed the arrangement. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency TASS on October 13 that supplying diesel fuel was "in the interests of Russia, the United States and global energy markets." Diesel prices in the US and many EU countries have risen sharply over the past 12 months. According to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), prices in the US have climbed by about 60% and now stand at $6.30 per gallon, equivalent to $1.66 (or €1.49) per liter of diesel. Diesel — Made in the USA But even if Russia were able to flood global markets with cheap diesel, prices would not fall nearly as much as they recently rose, something all of the experts contacted by DW agree on. Many refineries around the Gulf region have suffered disruptions or damage, while transporting fuel via shadow fleets and securing insurance remains costly, cumbersome and risky. Another key shift is that Russia is no longer the world's largest diesel exporter. In fact, it is facing its own fuel shortages at home. The US is now the world's biggest diesel exporter. In 2025, it exported an average of 1.26 million barrels of diesel per day, accounting for roughly 15.4% of global diesel exports. At the same time, Russia fell to second place with a 9.5% share, and that was before major Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries. Debates over export restrictions continue Besides the new US-Russia diesel agreement, Trump also recently floated the idea of US diesel export restrictions. But the idea was abandoned because it could lead to even higher diesel prices in the country, according to Samina Sultan. "There simply is not enough diesel storage capacity in the United States," Sultan said. "Production would have to be reduced, and then prices would rise again." Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video If the US were to impose export restrictions on diesel, buyers in Latin America and the European Union would be hit particularly hard. Since Russia invaded Ukraine, EU countries have increasingly imported diesel from the US instead of Russia because of sanctions . "An export ban merely redistributes the shortage; it does not solve it," said ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski. "Global prices would continue to rise, while refineries would scale back production as margins shrink," he added. Limited impact on US diesel demand Export restrictions aside, few people consider that the US-Russia diesel deal will have any big impact. According to calculations by the platform The World Data , the promised shipment of 2.2 million barrels of diesel from Russia would not even cover a single day's US diesel demand of roughly 4 million barrels. Even if all of the diesel volumes announced by Trump were combined, totaling 35.8 million barrels, they would only cover about nine days of US domestic demand. "I CANNOT OVERSTATE HOW MUCH OF A NOTHING BURGER THIS IS," Canadian oil market analyst Rory Johnston wrote in an all-caps post on X shortly after the announcement. Russia would normally export almost 10 times that volume if its refinery fleet was not being targeted by Ukrainian drone attacks, he added. Canada also supplies diesel to the United States. Roughly 80% of all US diesel imports come from its northern neighbor. Given Trump's verbal attacks on Canada and the ongoing trade dispute , analysts view the prospect of Canada supplying significantly more diesel to the US as highly unlikely. In the capital, at least three people were killed and 21 injured, Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS said. At least 600,000 people across the country are without electricity after strikes hit critical infrastructure in the Kyiv region and the north-eastern city of Kharkiv. The strikes come after US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that an "energy ceasefire" was in place between Russia and Ukraine. Russia's defence ministry said its "massive" strikes had targeted communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military. BBC Ukraine Correspondent Dan Johnson explains. https://www.monitor.co.me/background-of-.text: foto: Vijesti Share Tweet After entering Montenegro, Zinchuk described the Montenegrin border police on his telegram-channel as incompetent for failing to stop him, even though he is subject to EU sanctions. He must have known that his media activities would come under the scrutiny of the Montenegrin authorities. Evidently, he wanted to provoke his own public failure. This is not Zinchuk’s only setback; in late September, employees of his channel were deported from the Czech Republic. It can be assumed that he intended to demonstrate that his network in Europe is being monitored and cannot be used for covert operations On October 9, Russian propagandist Michael Zinchuk, his wife and three employees were deported from Montenegro, where they had arrived just two days before. Zinchuk operates several media projects, including his main telegram-channel “Rybar” with almost 1,4 million subscribers (telegram-channels are not widely used in Montenegro, but extremely popular in Russia). Zinchuk, despite his Ukrainian last name, is one of the most influential professional warmongers, who calls for fighting the war until the destruction of the independent Ukrainian state. Moreover, he is considered to be in charge of spreading messages that reflect the real opinion of hawks in the inner circle of Russian president Vladimir Putin. There is one question, which remains unanswered: why did Zinchuk decide to come to Montenegro. He explained that he had intended to make a documentary about economic and social difficulties that in his opinion, Montenegro would face after joining the EU. But that explanation contradicts his behavior. Soon after entering Montenegro, he published a post in his channel, in which he insulted the Border Police of Montenegro, which he called incompetent for not stopping him, though he is under the EU sanctions. Such a declaration appears to be extremely stupid, because Zinchuk must have known that his media activity would be observed by the Montenegrin law-enforcement agencies. Instead of trying to disguise himself as tourist as long as possible, he started with mocking the government agency, on which depends his stay in the country. The only possible answer is that he came to be arrested and deported. He knew that would be defended on the highest level. Spokesperson of Russian ministry of foreign affairs Maria Zakharova personally coordinated the activity of Russian embassies in Serbia and Montenegro in support of Zinchuk. The Russian broadcaster RT and media group Rossiya Segodnya, which target the audience outside Russia, highlighted news about Zinchuk’s arrest, because their editor-in-chief Margarita Simonyan issue a direct instruction to someone to do it. So Zinchuk did not have much to have much to fear. And he obviously wanted to fail publicly. By the way, it was at least Zinchuk’s failure in the recent weeks. In the end of September the employees of Zinchuk’s channel were deported from the Czech Republic, after they had too frankly talked with local journalist, who happened to investigate their activity in Europe. What seemed just a silly mistake can be regarded in another light now. It is possible to make a suggestion. Zinchuk wanted to show that his net in Europe is being closely watched and cannot be used for undercover operations. He and his employees are easily identified and exposed. It has been reported that after the election defeat of former Hungarian president Victor Orban, there has been a radical shift in the approach to the goals and means of the undercover activity in Europe. Supporting pro-Russian political forced has been recognized to be ineffective. It has been decided that more serious effects on public opinion can be achieved through social destabilization by actions of political radicals and acts of sabotage. Zinchuk might want to avoid participation of the members of his disinformation net in Europe in the execution of such plans. And the prospect of the implementation has become stronger in the last weeks. Because Russian president Vladimir Putin seems to believe that he has come close to making a deal with the US, which will give him a free hand in undermining the EU. In one of his recent speeches he revealed that he expects the EU to fall apart in the near future, but assured that he is not going to do anything to make it happen faster. Based on experience of Putin’s long rule, it can be taken for granted, that if he publicly assures of his inaction, he has already decided to increase his activity. Vladimir Putin is making the same mistake in his perception of the US president Donald Trump, as he made regarding his predecessors Barack Obama and Joe Biden. He thought that Obama’s feeble reaction on the annexation of the Crimea and instigation of the military conflict on Donbas proved that the US had no intentions and resources to impede Russia. It turned out that Obama’s administration just wanted the Kremlin to get stuck in the conflict in Ukraine to disrupt the economic cooperation between Russia and Germany (and the EU as a whole). Putin believed that Biden’s administration would not impose serious sanctions on Russia and provide meaningful military assistance to Ukraine. And he was wrong again. Biden’s sanctions were aimed at the restraining Russian economic development, not at the inflicting immediate damage on Russian economy. Due to that, Vladimir Putin was confident for some time that American sanctions were not working, and Russian propaganda was eager to demonstrate it. Now, the Kremlin wants to American sanctions to be lifted. And Putin expects Trump to do that, because he regards Trump as a potential ally in the confrontation with the EU. Of course, there is no love lost between the European Commission and the incumbent US administration. However, the American president does not want to destroy the EU. He wants to control it and obtain economic concessions from it. Putin, as many people who grew up in the USSR, do not believe that political systems of the Western countries are grounded on established procedures and formal rules. Unlike Russia, their governments do not need external expansion to achieve a legitimate rule, they already have it. So the goals of their expansion, even if they look unattainable like in the case of the current US administration, are grounded on rational reasons. Trump wants to make a profitable deal with Putin, but the American president could establish control over the energy supply of the EU, even without Moscow’s assistance. And Russia cannot help him in reaching his other goals, like reaching global dominance through the leadership in the AI systems or gaining control over global trade routes. So Trump tries to persuade Putin to come to an agreement and give US corporations a share in Russian oil and gas export. And the American president has nothing against putting pressure on Ukraine in order to facilitate negotiations with the Kremlin. But he cannot allow Putin to destabilize the EU, because the US president needs the European consumption of oil and gas remains high. And it means that the European economy should keep functioning stably. The US administration has already started to create grounds for justification of the upcoming cooperation with Russia. There can be no other goal of the so called “diesel deal” between Washington and Moscow, which was announced on October 9. The amount of diesel that Russia is supposed to deliver to the US under this agreement is insignificant. It has been stated that Russia will deliver 300 thousand tons in October, 500 thousand tons in November, 1 million tons after that and additionally 3 million tons. The US daily consumption of diesel is 500-520 thousand tons. Therefore, Russian export cannot make a big difference. Moreover, the US exports approximately 180 thousand tons of diesels per day. So the temporarily ban on export would increase the amount of diesel on the American market much more than Russian import. However, Trump does not need diesel; he needs an example of Russian willingness to help America in the time of need. He has already thanked Russia for its readiness to supply diesel to the US, and scolded Ukraine for ignoring American request to stop attacks on Russian refineries. It should be noted that these attacks could have been terminated, if the US ceased providing Ukrainian forces with space intelligence data. Trump does not seem to care much about Russian refineries. But he managed to demonstrate, that Ukrainian president Volodymir Zelensky pays no attention to American demands. So there is no reason to sacrifice American interests, refusing from profitable cooperation with Vladimir Putin, who proved to be an American friend. And if the cooperation between Moscow and Washington is established, it will bring huge results. It was reported for the first time in September, and almost officially confirmed on October 8, that the Kremlin and the US administration have been discussing a handover of the North Stream pipeline system to American corporations. Last year, speaking at the UN General Assembly, Donald Trump urged Europe to abandon Russian gas. The US administration is now planning to profit from its return, but now it will belong to American corporations, and Trump will have nothing against it. Germany eventually became dependent on Russian gas and dragged a large part of Europe into this trap. Now, after the EU made painful efforts to overcome this dependence, Donald Trump established control over the EU energy market. According to the data, 92% of German and 59% of the EU LNG imports come from the US. If the agreement with Russia is achieved (and it seems to be quite probable), American corporations will supply also pipeline gas to Europe. Moreover, Russian LNG will be certainly included in the deal, because its supply to Europe can be interrupted at any moment, if Trump decides to implement the law that gives him an opportunity to impose sanctions on the countries that import Russian oil and gas. By the way, American corporations can also take part in the production of Russian oil and its export to Europe, because the Russia cannot increase exploitation of its Arctic oilfields, unless American sanctions on the equipment for the oil industry are not removed. The show that Trump performed to justify cooperation with Putin can turn out to be very profitable. Besides, the US administration will tighten its grip on the European economy. At the same time, the EU security will be threatened by growing Russian activity, the destruction of the Ukrainian cities will continue and moral norms will be once again rejected by the current US administration. This dependence exposes Europe to the risk of high costs, price fluctuations, and geopolitical pressure,” the study states. The more Trump controls Europe’s energy supply, the greater the likelihood that the US president will leverage this source of power elsewhere. The national security strategy paper released back in November explicitly spoke of a goal of US “energy dominance”—one that “enables us to project our power whenever and wherever necessary.” The US appears to have already laid the groundwork for this. “We must acknowledge the new reality of American energy dominance under Donald Trump and view Europe’s imports with caution,” Professor Kacper Szulecki of the Norwegian Institute of International Affairs. He raises the prospect of a potential energy crisis, noting that EU gas reserves are currently very low, even lower than at the start of the war in Ukraine. “If a cold winter coincides with tensions with the US—leading to further price hikes and the depletion of reserves—we could face a truly dramatic energy crisis in the coming months,” Szulecki said. “Despite the rhetorical commitment to diversification, new EU legislation paradoxically treats energy from any country other than Russia as fully diversified.” Three-quarters entered via France in September: despite sanctions, Europe purchased nearly €8 billion worth of Russian gas in 2026. Europe continues to purchase massive quantities of Russian gas, despite the sanctions imposed on Moscow following the invasion of Ukraine. Import volumes are even reaching record highs. According to a new analysis by the German NGO Urgewald—based on data from the maritime shipping specialist Kpler—European Union ports received 12.18 million tonnes of liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the Russian Yamal project between January and September 2026. That is 9.5% more than during the same period in 2025. Over a nine-month period, no fewer than 167 shipments of Russian LNG were offloaded at European ports. That averages out to one LNG tanker every 38 hours. Another threat looms over Russian exports. On September 18, the United States enacted the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, legislation authorizing sanctions against entities involved in the Russian LNG trade. The measure specifically targets executives of the Yamal project and foreign vessels knowingly transporting Russian LNG, as well as the owners and operators of foreign ports that accommodate vessels subject to U.S. sanctions or provide them with services. The European Union now accounts for 85% of global deliveries from the Yamal project, which operates in the Russian Arctic. This is a significant proportion, especially given that the site’s global exports dipped slightly—by 1.3%—during the period. In other words, while Yamal shipped slightly less gas overall, Europe bought more of it. France plays a particularly significant role in these exchanges. According to Urgewald, nearly three-quarters of the Russian LNG volumes delivered to the European Union in September were received at French ports. A significant portion of this Russian gas reaches France largely because TotalEnergies holds a 20% stake in the Yamal gas project in the Russian Arctic and has a long-term contract to purchase 5 million tonnes of LNG annually. Furthermore, France possesses several LNG terminals—notably in Dunkirk and Montoir-de-Bretagne—that allow the gas to be received before potentially being transported to other European countries, such as Germany. Consequently, not all Russian gas unloaded at French ports is necessarily consumed within France. Since April 25, 2026, imports under existing short-term contracts have been prohibited. However, according to the German NGO, the impact of this measure remains very limited. How can the continued massive flow of Russian gas into Europe despite sanctions be explained? Quite simply because Brussels included transition periods for contracts already in place. Since April 25, 2026, Europe has banned purchases of Russian gas under short-term contracts. However, companies that signed multi-year contracts may continue to receive Russian gas until the end of 2026. The aim is to give European companies time to find alternative suppliers without causing supply disruptions or a fresh spike in prices. Consequently, a total ban on Russian LNG imports is not scheduled to take effect until January 1, 2027. This deadline could deprive Moscow of its primary market for gas produced in the Arctic. The proximity of European ports allows Russian LNG tankers to make frequent round trips. The Yamal project relies notably on Arc7-class ice-breaking vessels capable of navigating icy Arctic waters, even in winter. Urgewald is therefore calling on Europeans to go further by directly targeting the services that enable this fleet to operate. Russian oil output is at a 17-year low: Putin wants to tap into the Arctic’s billions of barrels but relies on two vulnerable vessels. With Russian oil production set to hit a 17-year low this year, the country is banking on massive Arctic deposits to pick up the slack. Yet, behind the ambitions of the Vostok Oil project—which could eventually yield up to 2 million barrels per day—this new Russian oil route relies on a handful of vessels and infrastructure that Western natio
